subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The monomer from which the polysaccharide starch is built is:
questions.explain: Starch is a polymer of alpha-glucose monomers joined by glycosidic bonds.

questions.q: Two monosaccharides are joined into a disaccharide by a reaction that:
questions.explain: Condensation forms a glycosidic bond and releases water; hydrolysis is the reverse.

questions.q: Cellulose is well suited to forming plant cell walls because its structure provides:
options: Straight chains with hydrogen bonding that give high tensile strength
questions.explain: Beta-glucose gives unbranched cellulose chains that hydrogen-bond into strong microfibrils.

questions.q: Compared with glycogen, cellulose differs mainly because it is built from:
options: Beta-glucose, giving a structural rather than storage role
questions.explain: The beta-1,4 linkage produces rigid, indigestible (to humans) structural fibres, unlike branched storage glycogen.

questions.q: A triglyceride is formed from one glycerol and:
options: Two fatty acids and a phosphate
questions.explain: Ester bonds link three fatty acids to glycerol by condensation.

questions.q: An unsaturated fatty acid differs from a saturated one because it contains:
options: One or more C=C double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain
questions.explain: Double bonds create kinks, lowering melting point, so unsaturated fats tend to be liquid at room temperature.

questions.q: Lipids are better than carbohydrates for long-term energy storage in animals mainly because they:
options: Store about twice as much energy per gram
questions.explain: Lipids are more reduced, releasing more energy per gram, and being hydrophobic they store compactly without water.

questions.q: A phospholipid is described as amphipathic because it has:
options: A hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails
A charged tail and neutral head
questions.explain: This dual nature drives bilayer formation in water — the basis of membranes.

questions.q: The bond that links amino acids together in a polypeptide is the:
questions.explain: Peptide (amide) bonds form by condensation between the amino group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of the next.

questions.q: The primary structure of a protein is:
options: The folding into an alpha helix
questions.explain: Primary structure is the linear amino acid sequence, which determines all higher levels of folding.

questions.q: An alpha helix or beta pleated sheet is an example of a protein's:
questions.explain: Secondary structure arises from hydrogen bonding along the polypeptide backbone.

questions.q: Tertiary structure of a globular protein is stabilised mainly by interactions between:
questions.explain: Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges and hydrophobic interactions between R-groups fold the chain into its 3-D shape.

questions.q: Haemoglobin contains four polypeptide subunits, so it possesses:
questions.explain: Quaternary structure describes the assembly of two or more polypeptide subunits into one functional protein.

questions.q: High temperature can denature an enzyme because it:
options: Disrupts the bonds holding the tertiary structure, changing the active site
Breaks peptide bonds in the primary structure
questions.explain: Denaturation alters 3-D shape (not the amino acid sequence), so the active site no longer fits the substrate.

questions.q: The full set of proteins expressed by a cell or organism is its:
questions.explain: Unlike the fixed genome, the proteome varies between cell types and conditions.

questions.q: Fibrous proteins such as collagen typically function in:
questions.explain: Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and strong, suiting structural roles; globular proteins tend to be soluble and functional (e.g. enzymes).

questions.q: A student tests a solution with Benedict's reagent and it turns brick-red on heating. This indicates the presence of:
questions.explain: Benedict's reagent gives a brick-red precipitate with reducing sugars such as glucose.

questions.q: In an aqueous environment, a globular protein tends to fold so that:
options: Hydrophobic R-groups face inward and hydrophilic R-groups face outward
questions.explain: This arrangement makes globular proteins soluble and creates functional pockets such as active sites.

questions.q: Iodine solution turns blue-black when added to:
questions.explain: The iodine test detects starch, which forms a blue-black complex; simple sugars give no colour change.

questions.q: Amino acids differ from one another in their:
questions.explain: All amino acids share an amino group, carboxyl group and central carbon; the variable R-group determines their chemical properties.
